You have to stand for something
It's a reminder: take it or leave it
Don't end up on the wrong side of that conversation
Trying your best is not enough; know what you are achieving
Islam at its core is emulating the Prophet
Only Allah makes the call that you have done enough
His greatness is in his humanity
He achieved the outcomes
He invested in people, not buildings
You can't make life's biggest choice on probabilities.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 13: Quranic Reflections (Ibrahim, Al-Hijr, An-Nahl)

spans.note: Gratitude is owed before anything else; ingratitude is refusing to acknowledge a favour and is punished by losing blessings unnoticed.
Failing to see a blessing as a blessing: Iblis with Adam's clay, and even Ibrahim with the news of a son.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024 Night 13: Quranic Reflections on Ibrahim, Al-Hijr and An-Nahl

spans.note: The cluster teaches showing gratitude, recognising blessings and seeing every blessing as from Allah.
Be a realist who acknowledges what is there, from family to appetite, before it is taken away.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 13: Quranic Themes, Appreciating Blessings

spans.note: Gratitude is itself a blessing and is shown by using what you are given for others.
Magnify small blessings, use them for others, and avoid entitlement.

lectures.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Disloyalty and Ungratefulness

spans.note: Ingratitude is the human default: pray in hardship, walk on in ease, forget who answered. Kufr at root means covering up a gift instead of acknowledging its giver; man takes everything with no thought of where it came from and no will to pay back, and on the Day what the hearts concealed will be exposed.

Arabic restatement: man wants much, gives little, never thanks, praises or remembers the gift. The cure is in the Prophet's example: thank people, show gratitude in worship, never remind anyone of your favours, acknowledge theirs.

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: An-Nahl 1-18

spans.note: The Quran asks gratitude for the universal basics, sun, water, livestock, your own existence, not for complex blessings; thank Allah for those first, and let a moment of gratitude at the new year become a lifestyle.
The basics are all Allah ever promised and everything else is extra time; gratitude makes you humble, kind, empathetic and motivated to give back.

lectures.title: The Implications of Knowing: Gratitude

spans.note: Knowing God makes gratitude complete, constant and active.
We recognize blessings as we lose them; be grateful now.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 3 (80:33-42) and the Opening of At-Takwir

spans.note: Gratitude is feeling you owe something for unearned gifts; it motivates action and is not contentment with mediocrity.
Ingratitude toward family leads to fleeing from them on the Day of Judgment; kufr in the surah means ingratitude.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Saba, Session 4 (34:15-21)

spans.note: Saba lost its barakah through ingratitude, a mentality that loss does not cure.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Saba, Session 1: Introduction, Praise, the Hereafter and Knowledge with Mercy

spans.note: Praise as an attitude: seeing strengths, avoiding despair, removing vanity, thanking people.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Fatir, Session 2 (35:3-7)

spans.note: The first command of personal submission is gratitude; it produces happiness, defines the ummah and starts with being grateful for existence.

lectures.title: Surah Summaries: Surat Abasa

spans.note: Ingratitude is the root of kufr; the unfulfilled command is to give thanks for life and every blessing.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat ar-Rahman: The Final Verses

spans.note: Islamic maturity is growing sensitivity to Allah's blessings; our debt is infinite yet we must give our best.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: Ash-Shakur (The Appreciative)

spans.note: Gratitude must move from words to action and extend to thanking people.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Qamar and Ar-Rahman Summaries

spans.note: Allah's gifts become blessings or curses depending on how we use them and whether we show gratitude.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Qamar and Ar-Rahman Summaries

spans.note: Allah's gifts become blessings or curses depending on how we use them and whether we show gratitude.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Ar-Rum (30:30-39)

spans.note: Crediting others with Allah's gifts ends in ingratitude; see everything as His trust.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (verses 12-15)

spans.note: Gratitude is the fruit of Luqman's wisdom; the believer's true station is gratitude, and the grateful benefit themselves.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 18

spans.note: The rising from ruku as the posture of gratitude, why we owe Allah everything, and how to train thankfulness.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 13-17)

spans.note: All of Luqman's counsel is a curriculum in gratitude; praise is recognition, gratitude is repaying the favour.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 20-24)

spans.note: Blessings cover people outwardly and inwardly; gratitude is the lens through which generations should see each other.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Insan, Part 1: Verses 1-4

spans.note: Count blessings from the time you were nothing; verse 3 frames the human choice as gratitude or ingratitude, with sabr only a temporary stand-in.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat As-Sajdah (verses 26-30, conclusion)

spans.note: Reflect on obvious blessings; taking them for granted and conditional love destroy the relationship.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 4 (33-44)

spans.note: We control none of what sustains us, from sprouting seeds to sunrise, so at least be grateful.

lectures.title: The Values of Islam: Perseverance and Gratitude (Sabr and Shukr)

spans.note: Gratitude is the core value, shown by using blessings for Allah and people, and destroyed by entitlement.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value, Episode 39

spans.note: Gratitude is the cure: credit Allah, ask Him to accept deeds, and focus thanks on shared blessings.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 2: Verses 17-32

spans.note: Gratitude is the debt man has not yet paid; kufr is denial of the blessing and its giver.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: Names of Provision, Al-Razzaq (The Provider)

spans.note: Rizq becomes blessing only when you recognize it.
Shukr means using provision as Allah wants, not just saying alhamdulillah.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 26: Sixth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Choose praise over resentment in hardship; even the ability to thank Allah is His blessing.
Prostration is the only way to express thanks for what Allah has given.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 29: Ninth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Being able to stand in prayer is a privilege that could be taken away at any moment, and should be met with thankfulness.
The right starting point in prayer is feeling fortunate and blessed to be standing there.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah #41: Self-Value Recap and the Essence of Vanity

spans.note: Hamd is the antidote to vanity: Allah is praiseworthy for everything good.
Muslims are a people defined by praise.

lectures.title: Descriptions of the Prophet, Part 10: His Names

spans.note: His very names Muhammad and Ahmad are tied to praise and gratitude.
His hunger at times is a reminder to be thankful for the abundance we enjoy.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 7: The Believer's Reply and the Farewell Sermon

spans.note: No one is owed anything; existence itself is an unearned gift.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Fatir, Session 3 (35:7-9)

spans.note: Gratitude is a whole outlook on existence and one of two preconditions of submission.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Yasin, the Believer of the Town (36:13-27)

spans.note: Familiarity hides the miracles around us and in our bodies.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 1: Verses 1-19

spans.note: Bounties like safety and sight can never be repaid, only answered with devotion.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 3: Verses 41-56

spans.note: Gratitude amid abundance is harder than patience in hunger.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 4 (56:57-74)

spans.note: Children, harvests, fresh water and fire are taken for granted though we control none of them.

lectures.title: Make It the Best Ramadan of Your Life

spans.note: Hardship lets you define and appreciate ease; real gratitude turns into using blessings to serve others.

lectures.title: Pre-Ramadan Halaqah 1: The Bounties of Ramadan

spans.note: Hunger increases appreciation of what you have and compassion for the hungry.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Asceticism

spans.note: Weeping over a simple meal and fearing being asked about blessings.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: How He Ate and Dressed

spans.note: Praising Allah after every meal and respecting food as a blessing.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Loyalty

spans.note: Remember and repay kindness, forget the good you did and the harm others did.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 22: Tahajjud

spans.note: Allah's favours are countless, and recognising that one can never thank Him enough is itself gratitude.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: The Inventive One, Al-Badi'

spans.note: We take sight, hearing and the sky for granted; modern life numbs us to beauty we should appreciate.

lectures.title: Ramadan Prep: The Philosophy of Fasting

spans.note: Fasting lowers unrealistic expectations so we notice blessings and stop acting entitled toward Allah.

lectures.title: Ramadan Prep: The Bounties of Ramadan

spans.note: Provision increases because appreciation does; entitlement toward Allah mirrors children's entitlement toward parents.

lectures.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Ra'd, Part 2

spans.note: People take constant blessings for granted and become entitled; the Quran keeps pointing them out.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: Al-Hayy Al-Qayyum (The Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining)

spans.note: Life is the ultimate blessing and kufr is at root covering up blessings.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024 Night 11: Quranic Reflections on Yunus and Hud

spans.note: Rejoice in blessings as Allah's bounty and use them in ways that please Him.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 30: Summary of the Quranic Clusters

spans.note: Gratitude means recognizing blessings, including hidden ones, and using them by Allah's law in service of others.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Mulk, Part 1: Verses 1-2

spans.note: Starting from zero makes every blessing infinite; the sick show how much is taken for granted.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Mulk, Part 3: Verses 6-11

spans.note: Kufr is refusing to acknowledge a favour, the opposite of gratitude.

lectures.title: Lessons Learned From a Year of Blood

spans.note: Personal problems are overrated next to Gaza; Muslims are the people of praise, and gratitude is shown by serving the underserved.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Mulk, Part 6: Verses 22-30

spans.note: Gratitude for hearing, sight and mind is using them well; few are grateful.

lectures.title: Stages of the Hereafter: The First Blow of the Horn (Day 12)

spans.note: Stop feeling entitled to life, notice its beauty, and recognise life itself as the ultimate blessing.

lectures.title: The Empty Space Ep. 6: The Sins and Solutions

spans.note: Alhamdulillah lived with the mind is the cure for vanity.

lectures.title: Surah Summaries: Al-Fajr

spans.note: Ease calls for gratitude and hardship for perseverance; the believer turns both into good.

lectures.title: Surah Ad-Duha Summary

spans.note: Remembering past rescues and the gift of guidance leaves no room for doubting Allah now.

lectures.title: The Beauty of Ramadan: Ramadan Treasures (Kunuz Ramadaniyyah)

spans.note: The increase in provision in Ramadan is a change of perspective that makes the same wealth feel like a blessing; familiarity with blessings is dangerous.

lectures.title: The Bounties of Ramadan

spans.note: Provision increases through appreciation; expect little from others and much from yourself.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 7: Humbleness, Part 1 (Vanity)

spans.note: Hamd as the antidote to vanity; even the ability to thank is a blessing requiring thanks.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 25: Fifth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Allah cannot be thanked enough, so thank Him in a dignified form and think of one specific blessing while praising.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 29: Tahajjud

spans.note: A single finger turns out to be worth a fortune, showing how much unnoticed blessing the body holds.

lectures.title: Arafat Lecture: The Day of Realization

spans.note: Feel Islam as a blessing rather than a burden.

lectures.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Greed, Desperation and Entitlement

spans.note: Entitlement is the opposite of gratitude: given ease, man says he deserved it, assumes Allah owes him good, and turns away. Kufr in these verses means ingratitude. The substitute is the felt sense of being blessed and deserving none of it.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman 29-34

spans.note: Gratitude is the base state of the believer; ingratitude means forgetting rescue and favours.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat As-Sajdah (verses 4-9)

spans.note: Opposites reveal blessings, and the first defect the surah names on our side is ingratitude.

lectures.title: Bounties of Ramadan (Arabic)

spans.note: Provision grows in meaning; belittling blessings causes their loss, a danger he highlights for youth.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 4: Quranic Themes 2 - Accepting Mortality

spans.note: Cherish youth, health, people and Ramadan rather than taking life for granted.

lectures.title: Receiving Allah's Bounty (Ramadan 2026, Night 9: Quranic Themes 2)

spans.note: Notice the unseen bounties in your life and respond as the people of Badr did, with thanks rather than boasting.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 20: Divine Signs

spans.note: The signs of the sea are for the patient and grateful; people sincere in danger forget Allah once rescued.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 7 (68-76)

spans.note: Livestock as complete blessing; gratitude is the first step without which the heart is dead.

lectures.title: Self-Value #39: Vanity ('Ujb)

spans.note: Gratitude is the cure: credit Allah, even for the ability to thank Him.

lectures.title: Self-Value #40: Vanity, Entitlement, Expectations and Mediocrity

spans.note: Gratitude is the cure for vanity and entitlement, and brings more.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value, Episode 41

spans.note: Praise Allah for your successes and praise others for theirs; this heals families and communities.

lectures.title: The Implications of Knowing: Moral Integrity (Part 2)

spans.note: The core argument: you owe your existence and everything in it to One who needs nothing, so gratitude, loyalty and obedience are the only ethical response, and ingratitude toward God is a moral breach before it is a theological one.

lectures.title: The Implications of Knowing #2: Moral Integrity

spans.note: Loyalty and gratitude to the One who gave everything are the only ethical response.

lectures.title: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick #3
lectures.series: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick

spans.note: Be grateful for good health, and for whatever health remains when ill.

lectures.title: The Implications of Knowing God: Equanimity and Resilience

spans.note: Every good, deserved or not, is credited to Allah.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 14: Remember Allah Much (33:41-44)

spans.note: Alhamdulillah as practical optimism.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Fatir, Session 4 (35:10-11)

spans.note: Gratitude and self-insight recapped as the two mindsets of submission.

lectures.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 11-19 (Fajr Dars)

spans.note: Say the travel dua with real appreciation rather than by habit.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 2: Verses 20-40

spans.note: Counting the fruit trees around his home showed him blessings he had taken for granted.

lectures.title: Achieving the Balance: Dua (Supplication)

spans.note: Ignoring countless blessings over one ungranted request is entitlement you would not accept from your own child.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 14: Quranic Reflections (An-Nahl and Al-Isra)

spans.note: Blessings belong to Allah, so they are used according to His rules.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 26: Quranic Reflections

spans.note: Ar-Rahman's refrain will not let you skip any blessing without acknowledging it.

lectures.title: The Five Categories of Community Investment: Mentorship

spans.note: Acknowledging those who mentored you is part of integrity; he credits the many who invested in him.

lectures.title: Quranic Stories: The Story of Qarun

spans.note: Saying alhamdulillah attributes achievements to Allah.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: Al-Hadi (The Grantor of Guidance)

spans.note: Be grateful for guidance and never use it to condescend.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 19: Quranic Reflections on An-Naml 45 to Al-Ankabut 45

spans.note: Being ashamed of humble beginnings is close to denying Allah's favour.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: Al-Badi' (The Innovator)

spans.note: The blessings of an-Nahl cannot be counted and are listed so people will be grateful.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 24: Fourth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Praising Allah abundantly in the words He loves.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 25: Fifth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Recognising the basic blessings already in hand guards against the race for more.

lectures.title: The Rituals (Reduced Concepts, Episode 4)

spans.note: Alhamdulillah forces optimism and gratitude, which improves life and resilience.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 26: Quranic Reflections (Al-Qamar 9 to the end of Al-Hashr)

spans.note: Unused or unthanked blessings turn against you; you decide the label.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 28: Eighth Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: The succession of night and day is given for those who want to remember Allah or thank Him.

lectures.title: Between June 6th and Rafah, Part 1

spans.note: If you have safety and food you have the blessings that matter; take your complaints to Allah in sujud and focus on your role.

lectures.title: Outreach, The Way of Our Prophets: Practising and Sharing Enlightenment
lectures.series: Outreach: The Way of Our Prophets

spans.note: Guidance is the most valuable gift and was given free; the way to thank Allah for it is to help others see it.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Mulk, Part 2: Verses 3-5

spans.note: Life is a free gift that modern pressures keep us from appreciating.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Jathiyah Summary

spans.note: Praising Allah deliberately lowers vanity and restores clear sight.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qalam, Part 3: Verses 17-34 (the People of the Garden begins)

spans.note: People take recurring blessings for granted until they are taken away.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ma'arij, Part 1: Verses 1-18

spans.note: Practical faith has only two states, gratitude in ease and patience in hardship; most people find more reasons for gratitude.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 14: Tawakkul

spans.note: Gratitude is harder than patience because you never know if it was enough.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 22: Second Night of Tahajjud

spans.note: Consuming Allah's blessings without thanking Him deadens the heart.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 24: Arrogance and Humbleness

spans.note: At the height of strength and success, the right response is to ask Allah for the ability to be grateful.

lectures.title: The Spirituality of Hajj, Part 1

spans.note: Most people only value blessings after losing them; the wise value them now.

lectures.title: Achieving the Outcomes: Goals and Accountability (Part 2)

spans.note: Nobody said alhamdulillah on hearing that Allah will not wipe the ummah out for its sins or let an enemy destroy it; we take for granted gifts the Prophet begged for and feel entitled to them.

lectures.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Forgetfulness

spans.note: Thanks for the ceasefire belong to Allah alone, as Aisha thanked none but Allah when her innocence was revealed. No gratitude to world leaders, his own country's included, until they admit they failed humanity and betrayed their consciences.

lectures.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Vanity and Arrogance

spans.note: Al-hamd is for Allah, not you: everything you achieved flowed from circumstances and facilitation He provided, so praise returns to Him.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 21

spans.note: The nafs resists true praise; gratitude requires shedding vanity and disgruntlement.

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: Al-Isra 23-39

spans.note: Shaytan's root fault was ingratitude despite being raised among the angels; the wasteful share it.

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: Aal-Imran 137-145

spans.note: Be careful of complaining that everyone has luck but you; what is not going well could go worse, and losing gratitude can lose you blessings you only recognize later.

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: An-Nur 54-57

spans.note: Knowledge, wealth, social life and peace are all present here; we feel the cold only from the car to the door while elsewhere people die of it.

lectures.title: Bounties of Ramadan

spans.note: Provision increases in appreciation rather than quantity.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 2 (13-19)

spans.note: Cherish people and blessings before losing them.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 18: Supplications

spans.note: Even someone unsure of God should want to thank whoever gave them life; hardship lets us recognise blessings.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 26 - Quranic Themes: Having Khushoo

spans.note: Guidance and prayer are unearned gifts, and recognising that is what produces joy.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat An-Naba, Part 1: Verses 1-16

spans.note: The earth, mountains, sleep, night, day, sun and rain were set up for us; 'Did We not' wakes us to blessings we stopped noticing.

lectures.title: Fifth Annual Iftar: The Day of Arafah

spans.note: We take for granted what is right in front of us.

lectures.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value, Episode 40

spans.note: Gratitude and confidence in one's potential replace the need for vanity.

lectures.title: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick #1
lectures.series: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick

spans.note: Health is taken for granted until it is lost; illness reveals how trivial most daily worries are.

lectures.title: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick #2
lectures.series: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick

synth.summary: For Sh. Adnan, gratitude is the felt recognition that everything you have came from Allah and that you deserve none of it; its opposite is entitlement and disloyalty, not mere forgetfulness. His key move is linguistic: the root of kufr means to cover, so ingratitude is covering up a gift so no one sees who gave it, and most Quranic uses of kufr mean denial of blessings. He leans on Al-Adiyat 100:1-11, where the war horse is loyal to a master who merely fed it while man is kanud, barren land that yields nothing however much it is watered; on the pray-in-hardship, walk-on-in-ease portraits of Surah Yunus, Al-Isra 17:67 and Fussilat 41:50-51; and on An-Nahl 16:1-18. His distinctive angle is that the Quran rarely asks thanks for complex blessings like career and family. It asks for the basics everyone shares, counted from when you were nothing (76:1), and tying gratitude to complex blessings risks losing it altogether. He pairs shukr with sabr: faith has only two states (70:5), and patience is the substitute who holds the line until gratitude returns (76:3). Gratitude must become action: night prayer as a grateful servant, service to the underserved, sharing guidance, and thanking people, since whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah. He balances that hadith with Aisha thanking only Allah, applied to the Gaza ceasefire: no gratitude to leaders who failed humanity. Perspective is a recurring tool: look at those who have less, and take your complaints to Allah in sujud. The theme grew from passing reminders in 2023 and 2024, often framed by Gaza, into a systematic Quranic treatment in the 2025 character series and the 2026 tafseer and An-Nahl khutbahs, ending with the argument that gratitude to the One who made you from nothing is the ethical root of obedience.

sections.heading: Gratitude means acknowledging the Giver instead of covering the gift
sections.intro: He builds the concept from the Arabic root of kufr and from the logic of owing everything to One who needs nothing.

subs.heading: Kufr as covering up a blessing

points.text: The root of kufr means to cover, as in village names across the Middle East. Ingratitude is covering up a gift so no one knows who gave it, and it is disloyalty to the One who put you here.
Most Quranic uses of kufr mean denial of blessings; denying the blessing of existence itself is the kufr of disbelief.
In Fussilat 41:50 kufr means ingratitude: the ungrateful will be told what they did.
Al-Hajj 22:66: He gave you life, will give you death and then life again, and still man is ungrateful. We enjoy what we get with no thought of where it came from and no interest in paying it back.

Al-hamd is not for you: everything you achieved flowed from circumstances and facilitation Allah provided, so praise returns to Him. Gloating over blessings is the strut Luqman warned his son against (31:18-19).
On Thanksgiving weekend he notes that Muslims need no special day: the ummah is known as the people of praise, and the Prophet will carry the banner of praise on the Day of Judgment.
The Prophet was Ahmad before he was Muhammad: Allah is worthy of praise regardless of what any one person has received.

subs.heading: Gratitude is the ethical root of obedience

points.text: Allah created you from nothing, needs nothing and cannot be repaid. Gratitude, loyalty and listening to Him are therefore the only ethical response, and turning your back on Him is a moral breach, not merely a religious one.
Prayer, fasting and zakah are acts of loyalty and gratitude rather than detached rituals, and parents come second only to Allah (4:36, 17:23) because after Him they gave you the most.

Shaytan's defining fault was ingratitude: raised from the earth to live among the angels, he still refused to prostrate. Al-Isra 17:27 calls the wasteful his siblings because they share that ingratitude.
Rights in wealth follow from the same debt: relatives, the needy and the stranded have rights upon you because you owe Allah and the money is His.

subs.heading: Gratitude and patience: the only two states

points.text: Al-Ma'arij gives the first command of the juz (70:5): in behaviour, faith shows only as patience in hardship or gratitude in ease, with no neutral third state, and most people find more reasons for gratitude. Patience is half of faith; gratitude is the other half.
Yaqub's beautiful patience (12:18) when told a wolf ate Yusuf is the model of sabr jamil: he knew his sons were lying yet showed patience without objection.

Al-Insan 76:3 frames the human path as grateful or ungrateful, and kufr there means ingratitude. He balances the two: sabr is the substitute player who holds the line when pain blinds you, but shukr starts the lineup and must return.
The believer's affair is all good: grateful in ease, patient in hardship.

sections.heading: The ungrateful human: the Quran's portrait of disloyalty and entitlement
sections.intro: He reads these verses as scenarios that name human reflexes, not to shame us but so we can change them.

subs.heading: Praying in hardship, walking on in ease

points.text: Harm means losing a loved one, wealth, status or an opportunity. In it the man of Surah Yunus prays lying down, sitting and standing; relieved, he passes by as if he had never called.
At sea every rival god vanishes and only Allah is called; brought safe to land, man turns away, ever ungrateful (17:67).
Fussilat 41:51: favoured, man turns away and distances himself; touched by evil, he is full of long prayer.
The Quran names these traits so we can transform, and he insists they can be changed: the Quran strengthens the fitrah Allah loves and asks us to shed other instincts.

subs.heading: Kanud: the barren land and the loyal horse

points.text: Al-Adiyat 100:1-5 describes war horses charging, panting and striking sparks into the enemy's midst out of loyalty to a master who merely gave them a little food and water.

Man is kanud to his Lord (100:6-8), land that returns nothing however much it is watered; he is a witness to it and only loves more. The horse knows it goes to slaughter yet loves the one who fed it, and our Lord gave incomparably more.
When the graves are overturned and what the breasts hid is brought out (100:9-11), the ledger of what He gave and what we gave back is exposed.

Fussilat 41:50 shows the person given mercy after hardship who calls it his due, doubts the Hour and assumes he will do fine with Allah. The philanthropist who gives one percent on camera and dismisses prayer fits the portrait.
Rejecting Allah over one ungranted wish while ignoring countless gifts is entitlement you would not accept from your own child.

After a long prayer the Prophet asked for three things: no collective punishment and no outside enemy able to destroy the ummah were granted, and the third was refused. Nobody said alhamdulillah for the two gifts; we feel entitled to what he begged for.
The substitute for entitlement is the felt sense of being blessed and deserving none of it. It is not heroic to be content when you have everything.

All parents want is grateful children, and spoiled children are disliked by everyone. If you demand gratitude from your children, why allow yourself entitlement toward Allah? His father, who uprooted the family to Saudi Arabia overnight, was raising grateful children.

The days alternate among people (3:139-140): nobody succeeds or fails every time. Be careful of saying everyone has luck but you; what is bad could get worse, and losing gratitude can lose you blessings you only recognize later.
Despairing of Allah's mercy is forbidden (12:87, 15:56). The Quran's cycle of greed, despair and entitlement is to be swapped for contentment, perseverance and gratitude.

Contentment is not the absence of ambition: keep zuhd for this world and ambition for Paradise. People want the best car and job yet ask only to scrape into the lowest corner of Jannah; worldly ambition is worthwhile only when it builds a better hereafter through generosity and service.

sections.heading: Why thank Allah for the basics first?
sections.intro: His most developed teaching, in the 2026 An-Nahl and An-Naba lectures, is that the Quran directs thanks to the shared blessings of creation.

subs.heading: The Quran asks thanks for what everyone has

points.text: The Quran rarely asks gratitude for complex blessings like status, a car, an office or family. It points to mules, donkeys, rain, crops and the drop you came from (16:9-11).
Thank Him for sun, moon, livestock, fruit, seas and mountains before children and job, or you risk losing gratitude altogether when the complex blessings are missing.
Many have wanted what you have and never got it, yet they too must be grateful, because the basics are shared by all.

Count blessings from the time you were nothing worth mentioning (76:1), through the mixed drop that became a being who hears and sees (76:2), not from where you stand now. On a home video of his fifth birthday he watched himself drop gift after gift, unimpressed, as children are by the 86th present.

The basics are all Allah ever promised; everything else is extra time after the ninety minutes. Be grateful for the air, the clouds, the blue horizon and the green, the small things that are the big ones.

subs.heading: Reading creation as a list of gifts

points.text: Night, day, sun, moon and stars are subjected by His command (16:12); the stars exist for him to enjoy, his cosmic iPad.
The sea gives fresh meat, ornaments and ships so that you may be grateful (16:13-14); mountains anchor the earth, and rivers, roads and stars guide you (16:15-16).
Is He who creates like one who does not? If you count Allah's blessings you cannot enumerate them (16:17-18).
Read the Book as Allah describing Himself and His giving, not through the words of theologians; it returns constantly to nature, as when He splits the grain and the seed (6:95).
An-Naba's 'Did We not' wakes us to blessings we stopped noticing: the earth smoothed as a nurturing cradle, mountains as tent pegs mostly below ground, and humans made in pairs (78:6-9).
Sleep is subat, rest, the root of the Sabbath whose people broke it by fishing (7:163); rest is what sleep was designed to give.
Night covers everything, day is for earning a living, the sun is a blazing lamp, and rain-squeezing clouds bring grain and dense gardens (78:10-16).
You cannot appreciate something without its opposite. Ramadan's hunger lets you define ease, and 2:185 ties completing the fast and glorifying Allah for guidance to being grateful.
Ramadan is a month in which the believer's provision is increased, and provision does seem to grow in it.

sections.heading: My problems are overrated: perspective without denial
sections.intro: Often speaking against the backdrop of Gaza, he uses downward comparison to reset what counts as a problem, while leaving room for honest pain.

subs.heading: Look at those who have less

points.text: Look at those who have less than you, not those who have more. His worries as a first-world citizen are trivial next to Gaza, so see what Allah gave rather than percentages.
Western Muslims, himself included, are the most privileged people alive.
Knowledge, wealth, social life and peace are all present here; we feel minus fourteen only between the car and the masjid door, while elsewhere people find a bullet instead of bread.
If you have safety and food, you have the blessings that matter.

subs.heading: Pain is allowed; ingratitude is not

points.text: He does not ask you to deny difficulty: take your complaints to Allah in sujud, then shelve them and focus on your role.
Uhud was a felt defeat and the Prophet went home missing people, visiting the martyrs every week until he died, yet he did not stop moving forward.
The questions asked of a Gazan father will not be your questions; yours will concern what you did with your comfort.

sections.heading: Gratitude must become action: worship, service and thanking people
sections.intro: Gratitude for him is a force that has to turn into behaviour, toward Allah and toward the people around you.

points.text: Aisha asked why he stood in prayer until his feet swelled when Allah had forgiven his past and future sins (48:2). He answered: should I not be a grateful servant?
When gratitude fills the believer's heart, his character and conduct change; it makes you humble, kind, empathetic and motivated to give back.
Start the year with a moment of gratitude that becomes a lifestyle of gratitude.
Gratitude is a force that becomes action: real thanks for blessings turns into using them to serve others.
Gratitude is shown by serving the underserved and being their voice; the ummah is one body that feels the pain of any limb, and this year proved it still exists.
Guidance is the most valuable gift and was given free; the way to thank Allah for it is to help others see it.
Carry a share of Islam's concern or become a burden it carries; whoever will not give a little will never give much.
The Prophet began calling his people with fewer than 50 followers; with two billion Muslims, changing how the world sees Islam is no more far-fetched.
Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah.
Do not spoil charity with reminders and hurt (2:264); the Prophet never reminded anyone of a favour he had done.

Near his death the Prophet said he had repaid every favour except Abu Bakr's, which he left to Allah, and ordered every door into the masjid closed except Abu Bakr's. Gratitude means acknowledging favours publicly.

Anyone who cannot name their mentors took without noticing. The Prophet was mentored by Jibril, his wife, uncle and grandfather, and paired the emigrants with the Ansar to learn from each other; the sheikh credits the many who invested in him.

subs.heading: When thanks belong to Allah alone

points.text: When Aisha's innocence was revealed and she was told to thank people, she thanked only Allah.
So thanks for the Gaza ceasefire belong to Allah alone: no gratitude to world leaders, his own country's included, until they admit they failed humanity and betrayed their consciences.
Read beside the hadith on thanking people, this is his balance: thank people for real favours, but never let thanks to people cover up whose gift it was or excuse those who failed.

khutbah_seeds.text: Covering the gift: kufr as concealing a blessing, the horse of Al-Adiyat against kanud man, and ingratitude to the One who made you from nothing as a moral breach; apply by naming the Giver of one blessing each day.
Thank Him for the sun before the salary: An-Nahl 16:1-18 and An-Naba 78:6-16 for anyone whose complex blessings are missing.
Count from zero: Al-Insan 76:1 and the fifth-birthday video, with sabr as the substitute until shukr returns, applied to raising grateful rather than spoiled children.
Do not walk on as if you never prayed: Surah Yunus, 17:67 and 41:50-51, applied to the week after an exam is passed or an illness lifts.
Should I not be a grateful servant? Worship and thanking people as the shape of gratitude, with Abu Bakr's open door.
My problems are overrated: look at those with less and the car-to-door cold, then turn comfort into service for Gaza and the underserved.

Blended with the Mumtahanah wording: in the Prophet is an excellent example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day.

hadith.gist: When the Prophet called for charity Umar brought half his wealth, thinking he would surpass Abu Bakr; Abu Bakr brought everything and said he left his family Allah and His Messenger, and Umar knew he would never outdo him.
Each good deed is rewarded tenfold, so three days a month counts as a full month.
Ka'b ibn Malik's account of staying behind from Tabuk, the boycott and the acceptance of the three's repentance.
The Prophet tells Ka'b to rejoice at the best day he has seen since his mother bore him.
Amr ibn al-As asked who was most beloved to the Prophet: Aisha, then her father.
The Prophet took Muadh by the hand and said he loved him, then taught him a supplication.
The Prophet wept holding his dying grandson and said this is the mercy Allah places in the hearts of His servants.

Umar acquired his best land and asked the Prophet what to do; he was told to endow the land itself and give its produce in charity, so it is never sold, gifted or inherited, and its caretaker may eat from it reasonably.
When a person dies his deeds end except for three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, or a righteous child who prays for him.

Among the good deeds that reach a believer after death: knowledge he spread, a righteous child, a mushaf he left, a masjid he built, a house for travellers, a river he made flow, charity given in health.
No one walks under the sky or on the earth more truthful in heart than Abu Dharr.
When Abu Dharr alluded to Bilal's race in a dispute, the Prophet told him he was a man who still had jahiliyyah inside him; Abu Dharr asked Bilal to step on his neck in repentance.
A man given charge over Muslims who does not strive for them and advise them will not enter Paradise with them
O Allah, whoever takes charge of any affair of my ummah and is harsh on them, be harsh on him
The companions would throw melon rinds at one another, but when matters became serious they were men of action.
He told an old woman that old women do not enter Paradise, meaning she would enter it young.
We will carry you on the son of a she-camel.
You joke with us; he said, I only say what is true.
Al-Miqdad drank the Prophet's milk, who then prayed: O Allah, feed whoever feeds me and give drink to whoever gives me drink.
Aisha's doll of a winged horse; she said Sulayman had horses with wings and he laughed until his molars showed.

Abu Bakr to Aisha: do you not know that when a servant delights in the adornment of this world, his Lord is displeased with him until he parts with it? She asked whether to give it in charity and he said yes, hoping it would expiate for her.
The Prophet prayed the funeral prayer for Abdullah ibn Ubayy at his son's request, with Umar objecting
Ka'b ibn Malik describing those who stayed behind from Tabuk as either excused or known hypocrites
Hudhayfah was entrusted with the names of the hypocrites

When the verse on being held to account for what is inside you was revealed, the companions came to the Prophet and said they could bear prayer, fasting, zakat and jihad but not this; he told them not to say as the people of the two Books had said, 'we hear and we disobey', but 'we hear and we obey, forgive us our Lord, to You is the return'. When they recited it and their tongues submitted, Allah revealed 2:285-286.
Rabi'ah ibn Ka'b, staying near the Prophet at night, woke to hear him recite the Fatihah, glorify his Lord in ruku and repeat 'to You is praise' after rising.
The Prophet told Rabi'ah to ask for anything; he asked for his company in Paradise, and the Prophet said: then help me against yourself with much prostration.
Ubadah ibn al-Samit's account that Surah Al-Anfal was revealed about the people of Badr when their conduct over the spoils was not good.
Mus'ab ibn Umayr was killed at Uhud leaving only one cloth; when it covered his head his feet showed and when it covered his feet his head showed, and the companions wept.
Thabit ibn Qays stayed home fearing his deeds were void because of his loud voice; the Prophet sent word that he was among the people of Paradise.
Had Zayd been alive after the Prophet, there would have been no disagreement about who would succeed him.

Abu Dharr insulted a man through his mother; the Prophet said: you are a man with jahiliyyah in you. Your servants are your brothers whom Allah placed under your hands, so feed them from what you eat and clothe them from what you wear.
Umar was corrected by a woman from the minbar and said she was right and he was wrong.
People are like mines of gold and silver: the best of them before Islam are the best in Islam if they gain understanding.
Mus'ab ibn Umayr was shrouded in a cloth that could not cover both his head and feet.
The Prophet saw Zayd, Ja'far and Ibn Rawahah in Paradise, with Ibn Rawahah's place slightly lower because of his hesitation
Who will buy this slave from me? ... but in Allah's sight you are valuable (Zahir).
The Prophet turned al-Fadl's face away from the woman questioning him at Hajj.
O Mu'adh, by Allah I love you.
Some eloquence is like magic.
Jabir sells his camel to the Prophet, who pays and returns it.
O Allah, I am pleased with him, so be pleased with him (at the grave of Dhul-Bijadayn).
What an excellent man Abdullah is, if only he prayed at night.
Ibn Mas'ud gave reminders on certain days only, as the Prophet did, to avoid boring people.
Umm Haram: people of my ummah sailing the sea in Allah's cause; you are among the first.
This prayer is not fit for people's speech; it is tasbih, takbir and Quran recitation (Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam).
The Prophet's address to the Ansar after Hunayn and his dua for them and their descendants.
They told As'ad to lower his hand, saying they would never abandon this pledge or ask to be released from it, and raced to pledge.
The long hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah describing the Prophet's Hajj from Medina to its end; the frame for both nights.

Before Hajj the Prophet named the places where pilgrims enter ihram, then turned to the horizon and asked Allah to bring their hearts to him as He did for Ibrahim; narrated outside Muslim with a reasonable chain.

Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Husayn visited the blind Jabir, who felt for his chest, welcomed him as his nephew, led the prayer in a cloth too small for his shoulders, and then told the story of the Prophet's Hajj.
The Prophet asked Bilal to give the call so they could find rest in prayer.
Abu Bakr: by Allah, if they withhold even a cord they used to give the Prophet, I will fight them over it.
Jarir pledged allegiance to the Prophet on the testimony of faith, establishing prayer, paying zakat and sincere advice to every Muslim.
The Prophet likened himself in this world to a rider who rests in a tree's shade and moves on.
The best of the companions are those who were at Badr, and the Prophet said the best of the angels were those who helped at Badr.
Abdullah ibn Salam, on first seeing the Prophet in Madinah, knew his face was not the face of a liar
Dimad came to cure the Prophet of supposed possession, heard his words of praise, asked him to repeat them and embraced Islam
Abu Hurayrah asked the Prophet to pray for his mother's guidance; she accepted Islam that day, and the Prophet then prayed that the believers love them both
Hudhayfah tells a later man who said he would have carried the Prophet on his shoulders that he was not there and does not know what it was like
Salman brought charity which the Prophet did not eat, then a gift which he ate, then saw the seal of prophecy and believed
The Prophet planted the palms for Salman's freedom; Umar's palm alone failed until the Prophet replanted it
The seal of prophecy was a small cluster of hairs
Jibreel told the Prophet to convey Allah's salaam to Khadijah and give her glad tidings of a palace of hollow pearl in Paradise without noise or fatigue.
'Abbad ibn Bishr, on guard while praying at night, was struck by arrows, pulled them out and kept praying rather than interrupt his surah
Umar heard the Prophet reciting Al-Haqqah at the Ka'bah and each verse answered what he was thinking
The Prophet told Uthman he would face a trial and should be patient.
Ka'b ibn Malik's own account of staying behind from Tabuk, telling the truth, the fifty-day boycott and the acceptance of his repentance.
Ibn Umar tells Abu Musa's son that Umar wished his deeds after the Prophet would merely break even, while Abu Musa hoped for reward; the son says Umar was wiser
A man told al-Miqdad how blessed his eyes were to have seen the Prophet; he grew angry, saying some who met the Prophet were thrown on their faces into the Fire
When Umar called Hatib's letter betrayal, the Prophet said he had witnessed Badr, and perhaps Allah looked at the people of Badr and said do as you wish, I have forgiven you.
When Uthman equipped a whole army from his own wealth the Prophet said nothing Uthman does after today can harm him.
Hanzala said he had become a hypocrite because he felt certainty with the Prophet but lost it at home with family; Abu Bakr felt the same.
Aisha asked that Abu Bakr not lead the prayer because he could not be heard for weeping.
The Prophet took a pledge from some companions to take from the world only as much as a rider's provision.
When the wealth of Bahrain arrived, the Prophet told the Ansar he did not fear poverty for them but feared they would compete for the world and be destroyed like those before them.
The Prophet held up a dead deformed kid no one would buy for a dirham and said the world is more insignificant to Allah than this.
Be cautious (wara') and you will be the most devoted of people in worship.
Love of the world is the root of every sin.
Whoever avoids doubtful matters has protected his religion and honour.

Hanzalah told Abu Bakr he had become a hypocrite because his state with the Prophet faded at home; the Prophet said if they stayed that way angels would greet them in the streets, but it is an hour and an hour.

Rabi'ah ibn Ka'b spent the night at the Prophet's door hoping to serve him, heard him glorify Allah in ruku and praise Him after rising at length, and when told to ask for anything, asked for his company in Paradise; the Prophet said: then help me against yourself with much prostration.
When Jabir wept over his father, the Prophet said the angels kept shading him with their wings until he was raised.

Allah spoke to Jabir's father without a veil and invited him to wish; he asked to be sent back to be killed again, and when told none return he asked that those behind be informed, so 3:169 was revealed.
People are mines: the best of them in the days of ignorance are the best of them in Islam once they attain understanding
The Prophet asked who would make the Quraysh hear the Quran; Ibn Mas'ud recited publicly, was beaten, and on returning said he had never feared them less.

The Prophet told Ashajj Abd al-Qays he had two traits Allah and His Messenger love, forbearance and deliberateness; asked whether they were acquired or innate, he said Allah created him so, and Ashajj praised Allah for it.

Khabbab, tortured on burning coals until he could only crawl, asked the Prophet 'until when?'; the Prophet replied that those before them suffered worse, that Allah would complete this matter, but that they were hasty.
Rabi'ah ibn Ka'b al-Aslami served the Prophet at night, was invited to ask for anything, asked for his company in Paradise, and was told: help me against yourself with much prostration.
Ibn Abbas asked Umar who the two wives in the verse were; Umar named Aisha and Hafsa and described how Makkan men had authority over wives while Madinan women argued back, and how he warned Hafsa.
Jabir looked at the full moon and at the Prophet on a moonlit night and found him more beautiful.
Aisha told the Prophet that a poet's famous line on a radiant face fitted him better.
Hind ibn Abi Halah's long description of the Prophet given to al-Hasan ibn Ali.

Ja'far ibn Abi Talib's address to the Negus: we were a people of jahiliyyah who worshipped idols, ate carrion, were bad neighbours, severed kinship and let the strong devour the weak; a man of known lineage and integrity commanded us to worship Allah alone, speak truthfully, keep trusts, honour neighbours and kin, and forbade oppression, consuming orphans' wealth and false testimony.
The first pledge of Aqabah: the Prophet took the pledge on the terms of 60:12, not to steal, commit adultery, kill, or give false testimony, and to answer any call with time and wealth.
A Bedouin wanted martyrdom, not spoils; if you are truthful with Allah, He will be truthful with you
Abu Dharr told he is weak and leadership is a trust; he would not lead even two
No one under the sky is more truthful in speech than Abu Dharr
When the Prophet named Abu Bakr to lead prayer, 'A'ishah objected that he weeps too much to be heard
Ammar said what the torturers demanded and the Prophet asked how he found his heart; when he said it was full of faith, the Prophet told him to do the same if they returned
At his death the Prophet chose the highest companion.
The Prophet recited An-Nahl 90-91 to Uthman ibn Maz'un, who said that was the moment faith settled in his heart; he had accepted Islam earlier only out of shyness before the Prophet.

Allah commanded the Prophet to present himself to the tribes; he went to Banu Shayban, and when their leader Mafruq ibn Amr asked what he called to, he recited 16:90, and Mafruq said he was calling to noble character and good deeds and that those who denied him had wronged themselves.
A man with ten children who had never kissed one was told: what can I do if mercy has been removed from your heart?
Abu Bakr wept so much in prayer that his recitation could not be heard clearly.
Dua is worship.
The Prophet greeted the martyrs of Uhud, Hamza, Mus'ab, Anas ibn al-Nadr and others, saying peace be upon you and that he would join them, God willing.
A hungry man was hosted by an Ansari couple who pretended to eat in the dark; Allah was pleased with what they did.
Abdullah ibn Salam recognised on seeing the Prophet's face that it was not the face of a liar
Dimad came to treat the Prophet, heard his opening praise repeated and accepted Islam for himself and his people
Ka'b ibn Malik's account of missing Tabuk and telling the Prophet the truth

At Bi'r Ma'unah Haram ibn Milhan was speared from behind while explaining Islam to the chief and cried that he had won, by the Lord of the Kaaba; the Prophet mourned the group and prayed against their killers for a month until revelation stopped him; the killer later came to Madinah to ask what he had won and accepted Islam.
hadith.source: pieced together from the seerah and the books of hadith

hadith.gist: The Prophet died asking for the highest companion.

A man told al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad he wished he had seen what al-Miqdad saw; al-Miqdad replied that no one knows how he would have been, that some who saw the Prophet were thrown into the Fire, and that they should thank Allah for being born knowing only tawhid.
Do not say 'if only I had done such and such', for 'if' opens the work of Shaytan.
No one did the Prophet a favour except that he repaid it, except Abu Bakr, whose favour Allah will repay; every door into the masjid was to be closed except Abu Bakr's.
Jibril told the Prophet to ask Abu Bakr, dressed in a sack after giving everything away, whether he was pleased with his Lord, for his Lord was pleased with him.
The Prophet met Suhayb at Medina's edge and told him his trade had profited
Jibril came to the Prophet carrying Allah's salam to Khadijah and the glad tidings of a house of hollow pearl in paradise with no noise and no fatigue.
During the Ascension the Prophet met Ibrahim in the seventh heaven reclining against the Bayt al-Ma'mur.
Ibn Mas'ud prayed behind the Prophet, who went on through Al-Baqarah, An-Nisa and Al Imran without bowing at a hundred verses; he admitted a bad thought of sitting down and leaving him.
Abbad ibn Bishr kept praying after an arrow struck his shoulder on guard duty.
Zaynab had a rope fixed to hold herself up when tired in prayer; the Prophet ordered it removed.
Do not complete the Quran in less than three nights; Abdullah ibn Amr bargained the Prophet down from thirty days to ten, seven and three and, when old, wished he had accepted the first offer.
The eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord, at the death of his son Ibrahim
Umar tells Abu Musa he hopes his deeds after the Prophet merely break even; Ibn Umar says his father was better
Salman weeps that the Prophet took a covenant that their provision be like a traveller's
Amr ibn al-As asks who is most beloved to the Prophet: Aishah, then her father, then others
A person who keeps praying (at night) will have its blessing show in his face.

On a cold, rainy night a hungry migrant arrived in Medina; the Prophet asked who would host him. An Ansari took him home, had his wife put the hungry children to sleep, extinguished the lamp and clattered utensils so the guest would eat the only food without guilt. Next morning the Prophet told him Allah was amazed at what they had done.
Haritha's mother asked whether her son, killed by a stray arrow, was in Paradise; the Prophet said he is in the highest of the gardens.
Two young men each asked Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf to point out Abu Jahl, killed him, and the Prophet told them both that each had killed him.
Abdullah ibn Mas'ud stood on the dying Abu Jahl's chest; Abu Jahl mocked him as a little shepherd and asked who had won the day.

Hudhayfah prayed with the Prophet at night; he recited Al-Baqarah, An-Nisa' and Al 'Imran slowly in one rak'ah, asking at verses of Paradise and seeking refuge at verses of punishment, with bowing and prostration close to his standing.
Ibn Mas'ud prayed with the Prophet at night and he stood so long that Ibn Mas'ud resolved to sit and leave him.

When charity was called for, Companions brought whatever they had, some a little wheat, some a single date; a poor man who had nothing announced he forgave everyone who had wronged him, and the Prophet told him the next morning his gift was accepted.
Abu Bakr, dressed in a rough garment after giving everything, was told Allah is pleased with him and asked whether he was pleased with his Lord

maxims: Be selfish in the right way
Islam feeds your ultimate selfishness
When you protect your brother, you protect yourself
If it's real, it's for everyone; if it's fake, it's yours
Ethics cannot be conditional
Never say: I would never be in that position
Knowledge is the saviour of the ummah
Read what? Anything and everything
Educated just enough to run the machines
An uneducated ummah will go absolutely nowhere
You can't cram the knowledge of Allah
My job is to seek knowledge and spread it

themes.label: Parenting and raising children

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: Hud 36-49

spans.note: A prophet could not reach his own son; do your utmost in educating, mentoring and being present, never judge parents whose children stray, and never use Nuh's case as an excuse not to raise your children.
The story is the Quran's example of a parent's deepest pain, now felt by parents who lose children to loss of faith.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Introduction, verses 1-5)

spans.note: Wisdom, guidance, mercy and ihsan are what upbringing needs; guidance comes through gentleness, never force.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman 21-28

spans.note: Raising children for Allah rather than for one's own entitlement; the limits of parents' rights.

lectures.title: Achieving the Balance: Between Leadership and Abuse of Power

spans.note: Children absorb domestic abuse silently and carry it into their adult relationships; staying 'for the children' harms them.
Raise sons to understand qawwamah as responsibility and caregiving, never as licence to abuse power.

lectures.title: Contemporary Issues: Sexual Overexposure

spans.note: Lowering the gaze must be taught at home and modeled by parents, or children will not practice it.
Unsupervised devices make exposure inevitable; parents must educate themselves and talk to their children first.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Tahrim, Part 3 (66:6-8)

spans.note: Prevention over late intervention, against enforced fronts and against bailing children out of consequences.
Children must learn to own the consequences of their actions.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 11 (33:32-34)

spans.note: Teach daughters and sons the etiquette of speech with the opposite gender rather than assuming they know.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Saba, Session 6 (34:25-33)

spans.note: Guide children, then let them choose and make mistakes.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Saba, Session 7 (34:31-37)

spans.note: Win children by logic, not power, and care about their hearts more than their appearance.

lectures.title: Surah Summaries: Surat At-Takwir and Al-Infitar

spans.note: Parents should support and educate, not control a child's choices.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 11: Quranic Reflections (Yunus and Hud)

spans.note: Do not judge struggling parents, and never let children grow up isolated from you or the community.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: How He Treated Children and Women

spans.note: His patience and play with children, never shouting or striking any of the many children in his home.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 20: Quranic Reflections (Al-Ankabut to Al-Ahzab)

spans.note: Tazkiyah has to be taught at home and early, so parents must learn it themselves.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 21: Quranic Reflections (Al-Ahzab, Saba, Fatir)

spans.note: Children who are always rescued never learn the value of decisions; let them face consequences.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat al-Hadid, Part 3: Verses 7-11

spans.note: Children need other adults to validate their values; boys need role models and standards.

lectures.title: The Five Categories of Community Investment: Mentorship

spans.note: Parents cannot mentor their own adolescents; children need trusted outside voices to validate what parents taught, or they drift.

lectures.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Navigating Differences

spans.note: Unlike his childhood in Syria, children here meet competing values outside the home, and parents give immature answers that lose them.

lectures.title: Tackling Contemporary Issues: Marriage (Part 3)

spans.note: Keep children out of marital disputes; their sense of stability depends on the parents.

lectures.title: Oppression on the Holy Land

spans.note: Children must be taught the narrative at home and in the masjid and be given hope so the cause does not fade.

lectures.title: London Muslim Survey (Part 1)

spans.note: A third of practising parents struggle to give children an Islamic identity, a red flag for the whole community.

lectures.title: Fiqh of Ramadan (Ramadan Prep Series)

spans.note: Train children to fast before puberty according to their capacity, without forcing them or making them hate it.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2024, Night 28: Quranic Reflections (Nuh to Al-Ghashiyah)

spans.note: Let children bear the consequences of choices so they learn to choose for themselves and the community.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Tahrim, Part 2 (66:3-6)

spans.note: Children need exposure to rejection, boredom and disappointment at home or they will lack the skills to cope later.

lectures.title: Seeking Knowledge: The Legacy of Our Prophet

spans.note: Children copy what they see; parents and older youth must embody learning so high Islamic and academic ambition becomes the norm.

lectures.title: The Empty Space Ep. 7: Sins and Solutions Part 2, with Q&A

spans.note: Teach children to observe their nafs with patient questions instead of yelling.

lectures.title: Surat Al-Ahqaf Summary

spans.note: Parents give all they can, yet two children of the same care turn out differently.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 15: Quranic Themes, Honouring Parents

spans.note: Birr does not license control over a child's studies, appearance or spouse; overuse ruins its sanctity.

lectures.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 21: Proper Representations

spans.note: Children absorb their parents' conduct as normal and are driven from Islam by hypocrisy and senseless rules.

lectures.title: Achieving the Outcomes: Defining the Metrics

spans.note: Children cannot be argued into Islam without modern examples; a child sent to the masjid without the example at home leaves after years of investment, failing every time.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (verses 12-15)

spans.note: Admonish children lovingly rather than command; it is harder with your own children.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 17-19)

spans.note: Teach children self-reflection and manners, and lighten advice with humour.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman (Verses 20-24)

spans.note: Inherited parenting methods are means to be reassessed against the goal of righteousness and success.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat As-Sajdah (verses 10-16)

spans.note: Without a relationship, teenagers are lost to distractions; parents must model prayer and come into the masjid.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Qiyamah, Part 1: Verses 1-5

spans.note: Children need help developing an internal conscience; external reward and punishment alone fail once the parent is absent.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Insan, Part 1: Verses 1-4

spans.note: Parents intuitively want grateful children and spoiled children are disliked by everyone; the same standard applies to us before Allah.

lectures.title: The Values of Islam: Sidq (Honesty) and Amanah (Trustworthiness)

spans.note: Children learn early that lies solve problems; parents must counter this.

lectures.title: The Values of Islam: Rahmah (Compassion) and Rifq (Tenderness)

spans.note: Firm consequences delivered with tenderness form children morally.

lectures.title: Our Communal Covenant: Your End of the Bargain - Participation

spans.note: Children copy what the older generation does; thirteen years of observation show the students still memorizing and attending as adults are those whose parents sat beside them in the masjid even when the parent had heard it all before.

lectures.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat Yusuf: The Brothers' Plot

spans.note: Yaqub's attention to the son being prepared, children wanting a parent's face, and children absorbing their environment.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat An-Naba, Part 2: Verses 17-30

spans.note: Do not coach young children in theology; once they reach the age of reason, teach both punishment and reward so they grow up balanced.

lectures.title: Bad Religiosity #9: Abu Mas'ud and the Whip

spans.note: Beating children and servants contradicts the Prophet, who never struck anyone; parents prefer not to be held to this.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 3 (80:33-42) and the Opening of At-Takwir

spans.note: Bailing children out and choosing everything for them produces adults without accountability.

lectures.title: Achieving the Balance: Desire and Fear, and the High Point of Love

spans.note: Children who never went without cannot appreciate what they have; it is not their fault, since they never knew lack.
Shielding children from life's pain and from the idea of punishment is unhealthy; teach them to deal with suffering.

lectures.title: Our Communal Covenant: Your End of the Bargain - Presence

spans.note: Bowlby's attachment work: one reliable person who shows up daily gives a child resilience; imagine a whole community that is reliably present.
Children become Muslim by belonging; fathers must bring sons and mothers daughters, consistently, because nobody will deliver Islamic education to the door.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 8: The Ruin of the Orchard (18:40-44)

spans.note: Do not teach children that the only reason they lack something is money.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 13: Musa Sets Out, Theory Meets Practice (18:60-62)

spans.note: Take children with you so they learn by example.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 15: The Ship, the Boy and the Wall (18:71-79)

spans.note: Teach children to question and explain your rules to them.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 16: The Explanations, and Living With What You Can't See (18:79-82)

spans.note: Children learn resilience by watching parents endure loss.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 6 (33:12-17)

spans.note: Parents curb toddler selfishness but often neglect other traits that follow children into adulthood.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 7 (33:18-20)

spans.note: Do not let inherited fear limit children's ambitions.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 12 (33:35-36)

spans.note: Double standards between sons and daughters push daughters away.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 20: Review of the Surah, Words That Hit the Mark, and the Trust (33:70-73)

spans.note: Yelling at a child relieves the parent's stress but teaches nothing.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surah Saba, Session 4 (34:15-21)

spans.note: Taking things away does not teach gratitude; some stubborn children are driven by being told they will fail.

lectures.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 3: Body Language

spans.note: A side point: humans are pre-programmed to read faces, so parents should trust their gut when a teenager looks like he is lying or in distress and deal with it rather than letting it pile up.

lectures.title: Achieving the Balance: Asceticism and Wealth

spans.note: Raise children to be as strong and wealthy as possible in every field, then to serve with it.

lectures.title: Achieving the Balance: Haram and Halal

spans.note: Calling a disliked haircut haram alongside alcohol pushes children to do both; teach them the real lines.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Waqi'ah, Part 3: Verses 41-56

spans.note: Let children experience hardship in controlled ways so they appreciate what they have.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: How He Treated His Family and Animals

spans.note: Play and honour shown to his daughters and grandchildren.

lectures.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Physical Description

spans.note: His varied hairstyles as a reason not to fight boys over hair.

lectures.title: Contemporary Issues: Principles of Gender Relationships (Part 2): The Rule of 5Ps

spans.note: Children who lack attention at home seek it online; parents should talk to them and know what is on their phones.

lectures.title: The Glorious Names of Allah: The Most Loving, Al-Wadud

spans.note: Children need love more than food, clothing or schooling.

lectures.title: London Muslim Survey (Part 2)

The command to warn his closest kin, which prompted the Prophet's first public sermon.
Prophets are sent to recite Allah's signs to people so they come to know Him.
Guard the prayers and the middle prayer: the middle prayer is left unspecified so all are guarded.

Read your book; you suffice today as your own reckoner: forgiven sins still have to be read.
Call on Allah or the Most Merciful; His are the beautiful names
Al-Hayy al-Qayyum in the greatest verse
Angels descend only by Allah's command

Falsehood cannot approach the Quran from any side.
Yaqub's beautiful patience as the model of patience without complaint
The Prophet's past and future sins forgiven, yet he kept praying for forgiveness
Fear Allah as much as you are able, listen, obey and spend; those saved from their own stinginess succeed.

Night prayer prepares for a heavy word to be carried.
The Prophet as the excellent model for those who hope for Allah and the Last Day.
Do not put yourselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger.

Ibn Masud after Ramadan: where is the accepted one, so we may congratulate him, and where is the deprived one, so we may console him

Hell will be brought on the Day with 70,000 reins, each held by 70,000 angels

Your Lord has gusts of mercy in the days of your time, so expose yourselves to them

Many a fasting person gets nothing from his fast but hunger and thirst, and many a night worshipper gets nothing but sleeplessness
Whoever does not leave false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of him leaving his food and drink

Whoever does not abandon false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink.
The Prophet's night prayer was eight, eleven or thirteen rakahs.
The Prophet held the Eid prayer outdoors with women, children and whole families attending.
Paradise adorns itself from one year to the next for the coming of Ramadan.
On the first night of Ramadan the gates of Heaven open, the gates of Hell close, the devils are chained and a caller calls seekers of good to come forward.
The Prophet led long night prayers in Ramadan, then stopped coming out lest it be made obligatory.
Men left behind in Madinah by illness share the reward of those who went out.
On the hijrah, a shepherd gave milk and Abu Bakr said the Prophet drank until he himself was satisfied.
In Paradise is a gate called ar-Rayyan through which only those who fasted will enter.

In Ramadan Allah opens the gates of Paradise, closes the gates of the Fire and restrains the devils.

Islam is built on five, fasting among them.
Whenever something distressed the Prophet, he turned to prayer.
Whoever does not give up false speech and ignorant conduct, Allah has no need of his giving up food and drink.
Many who fast get nothing from their fast but hunger and thirst.

When Ramadan comes the gates of Paradise open, the gates of Hell close and the devils are chained; whoever is deprived of its good is truly deprived.
Jibril made dua against one who reaches Ramadan and is not forgiven, and the Prophet said amin on the minbar steps.
Line up so I may praise my Lord (after Uhud).

Shaybah ibn Uthman's account of his Islam at Hunayn: the Prophet wiped his chest, prayed for his protection from Shaytan and told him Allah's intent for him was better than his own, then repeated it after the battle with a call to seek forgiveness.

When the first night of Ramadan comes the devils and rebellious jinn are chained, the gates of Hell are closed and none opened, the gates of Paradise are opened and none closed, and a caller calls: seeker of good, come forward; seeker of evil, desist.
hadith.source: Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah (he grades the chain sahih)

hadith.gist: Allah draws the believer close on the Day of Judgement, makes him acknowledge his sins, then says He concealed them in the world and forgives them today.

When commanded to warn his family, the Prophet praised and exalted Allah, then said that one responsible for others does not lie to them and that he was warning them of a severe punishment; he called each tribe to save itself from the fire because he could not do it for them, and told Fatima she could ask for any of his wealth but he could not save her from the fire.

Hadith qudsi: My servant keeps drawing near to Me with extra acts of worship until I love him; when I love him he sees, hears and moves through Me, and if he asks Me I give him and if he seeks refuge in Me I grant it.
In the last ten nights the Prophet gave life to the night, woke his family and did not sleep.
Laylat al-Qadr is to be sought in the last ten nights, with reports pointing to each of them.

The hearts of the servants are between two fingers of the Most Merciful; He turns them as He wills.

Companions saw in dreams that Laylat al-Qadr was in the last seven nights; the Prophet said whoever seeks it should seek it there.

The Prophet's household went months without lighting a fire to cook, living on dates and water.
Companions showed the Prophet a stone tied to each of their stomachs from hunger, and he showed two tied to his.
Whoever gives a fasting person food to break his fast gets his reward without reducing it.

The Prophet feared abundance, not poverty. The nafs devours whatever you feed it; take only a traveller's provision from dunya and direct the rest to the community.

themes.label: Activism, civic engagement and the path forward

lectures.title: The Five Categories of Community Investment: Advocacy

spans.note: Nusrah, from people, means advocacy: investing time, wealth, expertise and influence to stand by a righteous cause.
Concrete forms: media presence, organized lobbying with money and votes, and awareness inside the community.

lectures.title: Activism, Our Path Forward 1

spans.note: Definition launching the series: dedicating every aspect of life to a cause beyond yourself, with devotion, minimalism and understanding.
The Quran's term is qiyam, standing, against qu'ud, sitting back; the default in Islam is to take a stand for truth and against injustice.

lectures.title: Activism, Our Path Forward 2: Youth and Belonging

spans.note: Ideas cannot be bombed away; the ummah fails because its members will not give 100 percent to the ideas they hold.
Do your best even when you doubt the impact; history showed whose idea outlasted the other.

lectures.title: Activism, Our Path Forward 3: Our Compassion and Clarity

spans.note: The cave youths' prayer gives the two requirements of activism: mercy toward people and right guidance about direction.
Change happens only when a population takes responsibility for it; dedicated activism also makes for a better, happier life.

lectures.title: Pointing Out the Obvious 1: Qiyam (Taking a Stand)

spans.note: Qiyam is taking a stand: prioritizing the cause of Islam as an activist prioritizes a cause, and establishing a position that one's deeds will prove.
Each person finds a specific area of service guided by personal experience.

lectures.title: Tafseer of Surat al-Kahf, Session 3: The Youth Retreat to the Cave

spans.note: Taking a stand against a corrupt order needs courage, clarity and a written set of principles.

lectures.title: Assessment of the Current Events and What We Can Do

spans.note: Short-term activism is necessary but insufficient; activism must never die off.

lectures.title: Five Points to Consider During Difficult Times

lectures.title: Five Additional Points to Consider During Difficult Times

spans.note: Short-term advocacy is everyone's duty, but long-term work and advocacy, educating people to speak for each victim, are what change the next thirty years.

lectures.title: The Potential for Change

spans.note: The community has every tool for change, and what is missing is willpower. Change can happen, but it must start inside each person.

lectures.title: Ramadan: Our Turning Point

spans.note: Western Muslims cannot pressure politicians because they are disorganized; they must fund and build advocacy groups so their voice is heard and respected in policy.

lectures.title: Beyond Ramadan: What We Need to Do to Be Well

spans.note: Advocacy is the single goal the other priorities serve; the community lacks willpower and organization, not resources.

lectures.title: My Maxims, Part 6

spans.note: Change follows public opinion; campus encampments, community backing for students, and pressure on Western through academia.

lectures.title: Activism, Our Path Forward: The Pursuit of Guidance for All

lectures.title: Listening to the Divine: An-Nur 54-57

lectures.title: Between June 6th and Rafah, Part 1

spans.note: Muslims must consciously take back the reins of their destiny, be unapologetic about their values and work together toward common goals instead of in silos; the needle is moving only subconsciously.
Everyone must contribute in one of five domains: education, mentorship, outreach, advocacy, or unity and centralized finances; no committee or parliament should decide the community's fate.

spans.note: Centralize advocacy since political parties are not an option: coordinated international advocacy as after October 2023, and domestic civil rights advocacy, lobbying and representation on laws, curricula and parents' rights.

lectures.title: Oppression on the Holy Land

lectures.series: The Laws of Success and Victory

spans.note: Protests, boycotts and letters are a must, but the ummah only reacts and then returns to normal. Satisfying results need a long-term plan drawn from the Quran's laws.

lectures.series: The Laws of Success and Victory

spans.note: Muslims in the West hold the trust of pressuring governments that shape Muslim lives elsewhere; protests and emails were improvised because no advocacy structure or alliances existed.

lectures.title: The Intention Behind Ramadan
